summary:
Yemen's Penal Code 1994 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Article 264 defines homosexuality between men as anal penetration and punishes unmarried participants with 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment. The article prescribes a different penalty where the participants are married, and readings of the statute that treat the conduct as a capital offence circulate alongside the codified sentence; a visitor should treat execution as a live risk rather than a remote theoretical maximum.

Article 268 addresses women, carrying up to three years' imprisonment for premeditated lesbianism. Same-sex conduct is therefore criminalised for men and for women under the same code, with no consent-based exception.

The statute's reach is territorial. Cairo 52's country review records that the penal provisions apply only in government-controlled regions, while the rest of the country sits under competing faction authorities, so legal exposure shifts at front lines and checkpoints. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026 makes the same finding for events of 2025, describing Houthi and government factional control as determining where the law applies.

Rare non-enforcement does not equal safety. Cairo 52 finds that erosion of the rule of law, the humanitarian crisis and growing militia influence mean de-facto criminalisation is rarely enforced but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands. Vigilante violence is the practical exposure a visitor is most likely to meet.

Death sentences have been handed down in recent years. In February 2024 Amnesty International reported that two Houthi-run courts had sentenced more than 40 people to death, flogging or prison over same-sex conduct: the Dhamar criminal court on 23 January 2024 sentenced nine to death, seven by stoning and two by crucifixion, with 23 more given six months to ten years for homosexuality or spreading immorality, and an Ibb court on 1 February 2024 handed further death sentences. Amnesty demanded an immediate halt to the executions.

No legal protection is available to a visitor who is targeted. The state provides no protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, and the constitutional framework leaves LGBTQ rights unrecognised.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 2018 report Audacity in Adversity places Yemen among 14 countries in the Middle East and North Africa where zina provisions criminalise sex outside marriage and same-sex acts are explicitly prohibited. The report could identify no activists in Yemen willing to speak about their work, a documented gap that indicates the level of risk attached to visibility, and it notes breach of modesty laws used against expression.

The social layer operates independently of the statute. An IPS account from Sana'a in August 2013 records a gay man describing hiding his long hair under a hood as still problematic, in a conservative society with no place for him while the law treats homosexuality as punishable by death. Discretionary social enforcement sits on top of the codified penalty, so concealment remains the ordinary condition even where courts do not act.

The wider environment shapes movement and access. Human Rights Watch describes the humanitarian crisis as among the world's worst, with 19.5 million people needing aid, alongside the factional control that determines which authority a person is standing in front of.
localsOnly:
The Constitution of the Republic of Yemen, amended in 2001, does not explicitly address LGBTQ rights. It guarantees certain human rights to all citizens, but only on the condition that all legislation be compatible with Islamic Shariah law, so LGBTQ rights are entirely unrecognized in the domestic order.

The state provides no protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Residents have no statutory complaint route, no equality guarantee and no independent oversight body to turn to when an authority or a militia acts against them.

Residents in areas outside government control live under competing faction authorities rather than a single legal system. Cairo 52's review links the erosion of the rule of law, the humanitarian crisis and growing militia influence to a situation in which de-facto criminalisation is rarely enforced by courts but is invoked locally to justify civilians acting against others.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Article 264 mandates death for married participants is unresolved in the sources. The statute citation records a different penalty for married participants without stating it, while other country coverage states death for married men. The codified sentence of 100 lashes and up to one year for unmarried participants is consistent across sources; the capital reading is not.

Whether the death sentences imposed by the Dhamar and Ibb courts in January and February 2024 were carried out is not stated in the available material. Amnesty's February 2024 demand for a halt records the sentences and the demand, not the outcome.

Enforcement practice in Houthi-controlled areas beyond the 2024 court reporting is not documented in these sources. The inventory establishes that faction courts have imposed death sentences and that the penal provisions formally apply in government-controlled regions; it does not establish current routine enforcement rates in either zone.

No sourced information was available on entry or visa screening that could disclose gender identity, gender markers on passports or national identity documents, access to gender-affirming care, facilities rules, or recognition of partners. These are not sourced findings of absence, and each remains unverified for this jurisdiction.
